'''Logicus''' is a [[Prime Material plane]] in a sealed [[crystal sphere]]. It was nearly destroyed in a cataclysm thousands of years ago, so mostly exists as floating chunks of land and strange structures in a bubble of air.
Magic does not exist natively in Logicus, and planar travelers find that wizard spells above 1st level, priest spells above 2nd level, and all magical items likewise fail. What would be the ambient magic of the world is siphoned by the ''[[World Mind]]'' in order to keep the air bubble intact.<ref name="dttu49">{{b|Planescape|Doors to the Unknown|pdf=17290|page=49}}</ref>
The inhabitants of Logicus simply call themselves "units," and are fusions of flesh with mechanical parts, sharing a hive mind. Each unit is assigned a number, with odd numbers going to males and even numbers to females.
The four main fragments of the world are referred to as ''Modules'', and are:
# The [[Module of the Beast's Sanctuary]] # The [[Module of the Omenotron]] # The [[Module of Earth and Water]] # The [[Sealed Module]]
== Portals ==
The only known portal to access Logicus is the Third of the [[Four Doors]], a series of four portals which appear every 500 years, remain for two months, and then vanish again. The most recent appearance of the Four Doors was in [[128 YFHR]].
The Sigil end is the mouth of a [[cortelestial]] on the corner of Wharf Street and Bizarre Boulevard, in front of [[Beranto's Map Shop]] in the [[Market Ward]]. The gate key is to show no fear when stepping into its maw.<ref name="dttu48">{{b|Planescape|Doors to the Unknown|pdf=17290|page=48}}</ref> Another cortelestial appears at the portal's opposite end, on the Module of Earth and Water.
== Gods ==
Logicus has no known gods. The closest entities are the World Mind, the computer which keeps the system running and acts as the hub of the units' hive mind, and [[Logicus Prime]], the chosen life form which takes on the lesser role of managing society, hooked directly into the [[omenotron]].
== Background Information ==
* Logicus units appear to be inspired by the Borg from Star Trek.

[[File:Lower Ward map.jpg|thumb|right|400px|A map of the Ward]] The '''Lower Ward''' is one of the six wards of [[Sigil]]. It's home to the lower middle classes, the workers of the city. All manner of goods are forged, constructed, or otherwise produced here. It's also home to the headquarters of the [[Athar]] and [[Believers of the Source]] factions.
Long ago, the area used to be called the '''[[Prime Ward]]''', and was used as a destination for the [[Incanterium]] and [[Sodkillers]] to herd the [[Clueless]], in order to keep them out of the way of important city business. A number of restrictions were placed on the primes living here, until the [[Clueless Rebellion]]: some primes noticed a preponderance of portals to the Lower Planes, and began opening as many of them as possible as a form of protest. Fiends -- mostly the mindless sort, as the smarter ones knew better than to mess with the Lady -- rampaged through the area. Eventually the Lady did indeed take notice: the monsters disappeared (either Mazed or returned to their home planes) and the prime perpetrators were dealt with. The Ward slowly recovered, the Great Foundry built there, but the reputation (and odor) of the Lower Planes never really went away. Hence: the Lower Ward.<ref name="fw14">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=14}}</ref>

The '''lower planes''' (sometimes '''Lower Planes''') is a collective term used in the [[Great Wheel cosmology]] model to represent the [[Outer planes]] of [[Evil]] alignment, located across the bottom of the Great Wheel. These are [[Acheron]], the [[Nine Hells]], [[Gehenna]], [[Hades]], [[Tarterus]], the [[Abyss]], and [[Pandemonium]].<ref name="MotP1e-73">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|73}}</ref> [[Image:GreatWheel.jpg|thumb|600px|center|The Great Wheel of the Outer Planes]] The only other thing these planes have in common is the [[river Styx]] which flows through at least one level of each Evil plane.<ref name="MotP1e-83">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|83}}</ref>
The [[World Tree cosmology]] model rearranged, renamed, and reorganized the lower planes into the [[Fiendish Planes]] but some people still use the older term to describe the evil-aligned planes.<ref name="FRCS-311">{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|311}}</ref><ref name="PGtF-146">{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|146}}</ref>
==Inhabitants== A surprisingly great amount of [[outsider]]s travelled to the lower planes to do business with its natives, as the residents often possessed substances, items, and information that could not be found anywhere else.<ref name="TFTIS123">{{Cite book/Tales from the Infinite Staircase|123}}</ref> ==References== {{refs}} [[Category:Great Wheel planes]]

==Description== ''Manual of the Planes 1st edition'' describes various planes of existence, and what creatures characters might encounter there, covering the astral and ethereal planes, the elemental planes, and the outer planes. It also details how to survive in the planes, and how combat and magic differ under each plane's special conditions.
Jeff Easley's cover featured an illustration of a creature named in the book as an "ethereal dreadnought", although the book had no description or game statistics for the creature. This creature was later identified in 2{{nd}}-edition ''Advanced Dungeons & Dragons'' as an [[astral dreadnought]].

Schwalb]], and [[James Wyatt]] is a 4{{th}}-edition ''Dungeons & Dragons'' accessory for the core setting. It covers the [[plane]]s within the [[World Axis cosmology]]. {{quote|If you seek to stem this tide of chaos at its source, follow my lead—I set out for the dreaded [[Abyss]] on the morrow.—Lord Amgar the Bold, [[Paladin]] of [[Bahamut]] The planes have always been a place of great mystery and danger in the ''[[Dungeons & Dragons]]'' Roleplaying Game, and the new array of planes debuting in 4th Edition continue that grand tradition. Home to [[god]]s and [[devil]]s, [[demon]]s and [[genie]]s, [[fey]] and [[titan]]s, these strange dimensions offer unlimited adventure opportunities for Dungeon Masters and their players. Manual of the Planes'' explores the many planes introduced in the 4th Edition ''[[Dungeon Master's Guide 4th edition|Dungeon Master’s Guide]]''. This useful travel guide also comes in handy for players seeking to battle demons, devils, [[elemental]]s, and other iconic D&D monsters native to the planes. Richard Baker, Rob Heinsoo, and James Wyatt have collectively authored over 100 game products and novels.|Publisher's description}} {{quote|'''Adventure Beckons Through Planar Portals''' Beyond the mortal world awaits great peril, power, and adventure. Welcome to the planes! With this book, you can explore the magical realms of the [[Feywild]], the haunted lands of the [[Shadowfell]], the divine [[dominion]]s of the [[Astral Sea]], and the savage maelstrom of the [[Elemental Chaos]] and the [[Abyss]]. Every plane offers unique adventuring locations filled with unparalleled dangers and fantastic features. This supplement for the Dungeons & Dragons® Roleplaying Game explores the [[planes of existence]], including the Feywild, the Shadowfell, the Astral Sea, and the Elemental Chaos. In addition to planar monsters and hazards for Dungeon Masters, this book features new paragon paths, feats, rituals, and magic items for players looking for an edge when adventuring in the planes.|Back-cover text}} ==Contents== The ''Manual of the Planes'' is the authoritative guide to the new [[cosmology]] presented in the 4th edition of the ''Dungeons & Dragons'' roleplaying game. Like previous versions of the book the 4th edition of the ''Manual of the Planes'' (MotP) is primarily a lore book, focusing on background information on each plane it covers rather than introducing new rules. At the end of the book, however, rule mechanics are presented for new [[:Category:Paragon paths|paragon paths]], [[:Category:Inhabitants by race|races]], and [[ritual]]s. Information in the ''Manual of the Planes'' is considered [[canon]]ical to the 4th edition variant of the ''[[Forgotten Realms]]'' insofar as it does not directly contradict other 4th edition ''Realms'' sources. For instance, the details of [[Arvandor]] are canon but the details on Shom, which does not exist in FR's version of the [[Astral Sea]], are not. Similarly, the [[Feywild]] and [[Shadowfell]] sections are ''mostly'' apocryphal, since each campaign setting's variant of the [[parallel plane]]s is a reflection of each setting's [[Prime Material Plane]] rather than having details wholly unique to itself. The book is divided into seven chapters, as follow: # '''Exploring the Planes''' — This early chapter introduces readers to the 4th edition cosmology and explains how rules referees or "dungeon masters" might use the cosmology in their campaigns. The chapter also details how planes are characterized and categorized, how one might traverse the planes, and provides information on [[Sigil]], the [[Far Realm]], and the [[Plane of Dreams]]. # '''[[Feywild|The Feywild]]''' — This chapter details the realm of the [[fey]], a bright and lively realm known as the Feywild. Details are provided as to what races are commonly found in the Feywild, including a definition of [[archfey]], what the structure of the [[Seelie]] Court is, and what kind of locations a [[planewalker]] can expect to find on the plane as well as how to reach the Feywild. This chapter was primarily written by [[John Rogers]] # '''[[Shadowfell|The Shadowfell]]''' — Written primarily by Robert J. Schwalb, his chapter focuses on the dark and shadowy twin of the Prime, a plane known as the Shadowfell, brimming with necrotic energy. Details are provided as to what races make their home on the plane and what kind of locations a planewalker might find while traversing to the plane, as well as how to reach it in the first place. # '''[[Elemental Chaos|The Elemental Chaos]]''' — The Elemental Chaos is described here by James Wyatt. How to reach the Chaos as well as what locations and [[elemental realm]]s a planewalker might visit are described here, as are the various races that make their home on the plane. # '''[[Astral Sea|The Astral Sea]]''' — Written by Richard Baker, this chapter describes the Astral Sea and its inhabitants. The most prominent [[astral dominion]]s are listed, as are the types of races who commonly make their homes on the plane. The chapter also describes how one might travel the Astral Sea. # '''[[:Category:Outsiders|Monsters of the Planes]]''' — An alphabetical listing similar to that in the ''[[Monster Manual 4th edition|Monster Manual]]'' is provided here, from [[air archon]]s to [[raavasta]]. Included alongside more "mundane" monsters are the [[demon lord]]s [[Baphomet]] and [[Graz'zt]] as well as the [[archdevil]] [[Dispater]]. Rudimentary rules for playing a [[bladeling]] are also provided. # '''[[Planewalker|Planar Characters]]''' The final chapter provides information useful for players, including new paragon paths, such as the [[doomguard marauder]] or the [[Malec-Keth janissary]], as well as new rituals and items. ==Index== {{IndexLink|Click here for page index}} ===Creatures=== {{P|[[Air archon|archon, air]]|114}} • {{P|[[astral dreadnought]]|115}} • {{P|[[bladeling]]|116}} • {{P|[[howling blade]]|119}} • {{P|[[demon]]|120}} ({{P|[[canoloth]]|120}} • {{P|[[chasme]]|121}} • {{P|[[shadow demon]]|122}} • {{P|[[solamith]]|123}}) • {{P|[[devil]]|124}} ({{P|[[Hamatula|barbed devil]]|124}} • {{P|[[brazen devil]]|125}} • {{P|[[Excruciarch|pain devil]]|126}} • {{P|[[storm devil]]|127}}) • {{P|[[keeper (creature)|keeper]]|134}} • {{P|[[korred]]|135}} • {{P|[[raavasta]]|136}} ==Appendix== ===External Links=== {{External link disclaimer}} * {{FRW}} * {{DMsGuild}} * {{DriveThruRPG}} [[Category:Planes sourcebooks]] [[Category:4th edition sourcebooks]] [[Category:Sourcebooks]] [[Category:Works by James Wyatt]] [[Category:Works by John Rogers]] [[Category:Works by Richard Baker]] [[Category:Works by Robert J. [[File:Market Ward map.jpg|thumb|right|250px|A map of the Ward]] The '''Market Ward''' is one of the six wards of [[Sigil]]. It's home to traders and salesman, as well as the [[Free League]] faction.
After the consolidation of the factions, the power of the guilds in the [[Guildhall Ward]] was usurped. Most withered away, or moved out of Sigil. Without the guilds, Guildhall became gradually less distinguishable from its neighbor, the Market Ward, and most Cagers consider them two halves of one whole.<ref name="fw19">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=19}}</ref> For convenience, most residents consider Duskgate Road the informal boundary between the two.<ref name="itc87">{{b|Planescape|In the Cage: A Guide to Sigil|pdf=17274|page=87}}</ref>
: ''Note that {{b|Planescape|Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse}} uses the "Market Ward" to refer to both the Market and Guildhall Wards; presumably the lines have blurred further and the two wards are no longer referred to separately. For compatibility with older products, this wiki keeps the two entries separate. Please see the [[Guildhall Ward]] article for further information.''
== Location ==
The Market Ward was next to [[The Lady's Ward]] on one side, and the [[Guildhall Ward]] on the other. There's only one real distinct district in the area (two, if including the Great Bazaar as a district):

It was owned by the [[Pharaonic pantheon|Pharaonic]]{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|86}} and [[Mulhorandi pantheon|Mulhorandi]] solar [[deity]] [[Ra]]{{Cite book/Powers & Pantheons|94}} and later his son [[Horus-Re]].{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|157}} ==Description== During daylight hours this ship had the form of a tremendous [[galley]] of war and was known by the moniker of '''''Matet'''''. During the night, the ship would transform into a barge, sometimes said to be a funerary barge,{{Cite book/Planes of Law/Arcadia|19}}{{Cite book/Legends & Lore 2nd edition|92}} and took on the moniker of '''''Semktet'''''. The ship was notably crafted from part of a sun (though not “[[the sun]]” of [[Realmspace]]). ==Powers== This ship was capable of sailing or floating through the sky, [[Wildspace]], and even the [[Astral Plane]]. The ship was also said to be incapable of being affected by [[magic]], but in reality it radiated an ''[[anti-magic shell]]'' that prevented anyone but its owner from casting [[spell]]s, and due to its solar nature was surrounded by an aura of flames that would harm any being who touched the ship without its owner's permission. Other abilities of the ship that could be activated at the command of its owner included being able to go ''[[invisibility|invisible]]'', assume a ''[[wraithform]]'', or ''[[plane shift]]''. And thrice per day, its owner could command the ship to fire a devastating bolt of solar fire. ==Location== In both the [[Great Wheel cosmology|Great Wheel]] and [[World Tree cosmology|World Tree]] [[cosmologies]], this ship was said to be found on [[Heliopolis]]. There its owner, whether Ra or Horus-Re, would ride it daily across the sky and with it carry the scorching sun that brought light to the [[plane]]. In the Great Wheel conception of Heliopolis, during the night Semktet was said to briefly provide light to [[Memphiria]], the [[divine domain]] of [[Osiris]]. Prior to coming to Realmspace, the [[avatar]] of Ra would often manifest alongside this ship. And following the [[Time of Troubles]], Horus-Re would often manifest the ship on [[Toril]] alongside his avatar. ==Inhabitants== Besides either of the ship's divine owners, this solar barge was inhabited and manned by a number of their [[proxies]]. ==History== In ancient times, the great serpent [[Apep]] would regularly assail Mantet{{Cite book/Deities and Demigods|136-138}} on behalf of the god [[Set]], in an effort to destroy the sunlight it carried and plunge the Pharaonic pantheon into [[chaos]]. On the world of Toril, in the year {{Yearlink|-4366}},{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|26}} the mages of a nation on the continent of [[Faerûn]] known as the [[Imaskar Empire]] sought to replenish their population after a devastating plague known as the [[Silent Death]]. To this end they opened two great ''[[gate]]s'' to [[Earth|another world]],{{Cite book/Powers & Pantheons|2,94}} using what they called the [[Bukhara Spires]],{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|18}} and kidnapped numerous [[human]]s from two lands in two different periods of time. One of these lands was [[Wikipedia:Ancient Egypt|a desert]], given life by the seasonal flooding of [[Wikipedia:Nile|a great river]], whose people worshiped the Pharaonic pantheon. The kidnapped humans would pray hard to the Pharaonic deities for salvation, but it was no use, as the divine scorning [[Artificer (Imaskari)|wizards of Imaskar]] had closed all their ''gates'' and put up wards to prevent their prayers from being heard.{{Cite book/Lost Empires of Faerûn|61}} The [[Overgod]] of Realmspace, [[Lord Ao]], heard the prayers of these people and they contacted [[Ptah]], an ancient deity of Wildspace with ties to the Pharaonic pantheon. At Lord Ao's request, Ptah returned to the home world of these people and informed the rest of his pantheon how they could circumvent the divine ward of the Imaskari, thus allowing them to come to the aid of their enslaved worshipers. Most of the Pharaonic deities went on to create powerful avatars known as manifestations (with Ra naming his Re) and traveled as them upon Matet through Wildspace under the shining guidance of Ptah’s ''[[Beacon of Light]]''.{{Cite book/Volo's Guide to All Things Magical|95-96}} Eventually, they reached the [[crystal sphere]] of Realmspace and its world of Toril, where Matet made landing upon the highest peaks of the [[Teyla Shan]], a mountain range on the northeastern edge of the Imaskari Empire. There it landed close to the [[Galley of the Gods]], a ship that the avatars of the later [[Untheric pantheon]] likewise used to access Realmspace. In the 11{{th}} century [[DR]], in [[Battle of the Gods|a major battle]] that was part of a larger conflict in the [[Old Empires]] region known as the [[Orcgate Wars]], Re died from injuries he received from the [[orc]] deity [[Gruumsh]]. Re transferred his divine power to his son Horus, who was from then on known as Horus-Re and inherited his father's ship. ==Appendix== ===Notes=== {{Notes}} ===External Links=== * {{Wikipedia external link|Solar barque}} ===References=== {{Refs}} [[Category:Artifacts]] [[Category:Barges]] [[Category:Demiplanes]] [[Category:Galleys]] [[Category:Horus-Rethan items]] [[Category:Ships]] [[Category:Vessels]]

==Description== This realm was a great cavern, with the ruins of what looked to be a once mighty city standing above it.<ref name="APPttO-p30" /> Within the cavern itself, there were a variety of [[hourglass]]es scattered about.<ref name="APPttO-p30" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" /> According to dragon theology,<ref name="APPttO-p30" /> these measured the life of every dragon throughout the [[multiverse]],<ref name="APPttO-p30" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" /> as well as every other creature that was considered a member of [[dragonkind]].<ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" />
==Cosmography== This divine realm was situated in the [[Outlands]],<ref name="APPttO-p30" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" /><ref name="CotD-p121">{{Cite book/Cult of the Dragon|121}}</ref> near the [[Dwarvish Mountain]].<ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" /> ===Planar Traits=== Reflections were incapable of being present while in this realm, even from the smoothest of water.<ref name="drag205-p51" />
==History== During the reign of King [[Azoun Obarskyr IV]], a [[half-elven]] [[paladin]] of [[Oghma]] from [[Cormyr]] was dispatched on a mission to explore the [[planes of existence]] beyond [[Toril]]. The paladin's name was [[Ambran|Ambran the Seeker]], and excerpts from his journal still survived to the [[Present Age]]. In volume 7, Ambran described how he hired a [[bariaur]] guide named [[Glin]] to take him from [[Sigil]] to the Outlands.<ref>{{Cite dragon/204/The Plane Truth Part II: A Journey to the Outlands|31}}</ref>
In his last journal, Ambran described having spent some indeterminate amount of time in the Mausoleum, having lost sense of how long he had spent there. Glin impatiently urged the paladin for the two of them to leave, worried that Chronepsis might soon tire of their presence, and though he felt a pang of reluctance Ambran agreed. On the following day, he wonders in his journal if the dragon god had even truly been aware of their presence in his realm.<ref name="drag205-p51">{{Cite dragon/204/The Plane Truth Part II: A Journey to the Outlands|51}}</ref>
==Inhabitants== This realm was devoid of any living inhabitants or [[petitioner]]s, being home to only Chronepsis.<ref name="APPttO-p30" /><ref name="PCS.SaB-p18" />
==Rumors & Legends== Some claimed that the Mausoleum existed simultaneously on the Outlands, the [[Negative Material plane]], and the [[Demiplane of Shadow]]. While others would tell of it being the same structure as the [[Mausoleum of Pain]], divine realm of [[Faluzure]] in [[Carceri]], and somehow coexisting on both [[planes of existence]].<ref name="CotD-p121" />

{{Quote |Mechanus is a place of ''rules''. Law and process. ''Organization above all''. The denizens of this place disagree on how order is to be ''maintained'', but in the end we ''all'' serve its ''structure''. Without structure, we are ''nothing''. |A [[parai]], a creature native to Nirvana.<ref name="EABG11">{{Cite comic/Evil at Baldur's Gate 3|11}}</ref> }}
==Description== {{fq | text = You are hereby exiled from the glory that is Mechanus! If you should ever return, even greater punishments shall be leveled against you, including but not limited to severe fines, imprisonment, hard labor, loss of limbs, loss of sight, [[geas]] magic, modron cleaning, modron counting, legal file alphabetization... | source = A judge (fortunately) banishing someone from Mechanus.<ref name="EBG3p18">{{Cite comic/Evil at Baldur's Gate 3|18}}</ref> | float = left | width = }} This plane was filled with an infinite number of country-sized circular interlocking gears which were habitable on one or both sides. These great flat wheels were at least {{SI|1000|mi|k|long=yes}} in diameter and had teeth that meshed at right angles, all turning slowly in synchronicity. Each disk had its own gravity that operated in a sphere circumscribing it exactly and pulling normal to the top and bottom surfaces.<ref name="MotP1e-84-85" /> The void between the gears was filled with air, allowing easy flight. Outside a gravity sphere, objects would feel only very weak attraction to nearby disks.<ref name="MotP1e-84-85" />
A plane of Law and order, Nirvana had equal amounts of light and dark, heat and cold, and equal measures of the four elements. There was a place for everything and everything was in its place. Even individuals living here existed to fit into the greater scheme of things and thus achieve a perfect society. There was no pain, but the only pleasure was in successfully filling a role like a gear in a machine. Passion, fantasy, and illusion did not exist here, except for what might be brought in by visitors, and any who tried to foment individualism or stir passions for a cause soon found they were not well received.<ref name="MotP1e-84-85" />
Nirvana was connected to the [[Prime Material Plane]]s via the [[Astral Plane]], and to the [[Outer Planes]] of [[Arcadia]], [[Acheron]], and [[Concordant Opposition]] by portals which appeared once every revolution of the gears they belonged to. The period of rotation depended on the size of the gear, but a typical period was twenty days. The portals stayed open for exactly one day. There was one portal to Concordant Opposition, located at the center of the featureless bottom side of a large gear, that was continually open.<ref name="MotP1e-84-85" />
==Inhabitants== The only creatures native to Nirvana were the [[modron]]s, a race of beings organized in a rigid caste system and ruled by [[Primus]], the One and the Prime. The most common modrons were the monodrones,<ref name="MMII1e-86" /> single-function drones used as common laborers, servants, or soldiers.<ref name="MMII1e-87">{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|87}}</ref>

==History== [[File:Modrons-mechanus-5e.jpg|thumb|230px|''Adventurers hiding from the Great [[Modron]] March departing from Mechanus.'']] After [[Orcus]] killed Primus and triggered an unexpected [[Great Modron March]], he left the [[Energy Pool]] in [[Regulus]] to search for the ''[[Wand of Orcus]]'', leaving the way open for a [[secundus]] to be promoted into the new Primus. However, prolonged contact with the Pool caused Orcus's [[evil]] influence to taint a fraction of the modrons. One tainted secundus disputed the ascension of any one of the other three and rebelled, leaving Mechanus and taking almost a million modrons with him. The dissidents settled a modron colony in [[Acheron]], where they regrouped to later attempt to retake the plane. This schism crippled the modron race and paved the way for a [[formian]] invasion of Mechanus.<ref name="Dr354-p36">{{Cite dragon/354/Return of the Modrons|36}}</ref>
In the late 15{{th}} century [[DR]], the [[wild mage]] [[Delina]] was sent to Mechanus by [[Martikay]] in order to search for a way to cure her from her wild magic surges. After interacting with several modrons, she was brought to trial by the [[Fraternity of Order]] at Regulus under charges of being an agent of chaos. She was found guilty and summarily sentenced to exile from the plane. The experience allowed Delina to better understand, rather than control, her wild magic.<ref name="EBG3">{{Cite comic/Evil at Baldur's Gate 3}}</ref>

Justice purges evil and makes them better. Once everyone's been cleansed, the multiverse reaches perfection. == History == In the [[Great Upheaval]] of [[503 BFHR]], as the city's 50 factions try to reduce their number down to a mere 15, two factions -- the [[Sodkillers]], a lawful evil group of hired muscle who would avenge perceived "wrongs" for the right amount of jink, and the [[Sons of Mercy]], a lawful good group who would find loopholes for the wrongfully accused -- joined up as a single faction dedicated to justice. and the Mercykillers were born. They created the [[Eight Tenets of Justice]], the foundational document for the new faction. * [[174 BFHR]]: An [[Revolutionary League|Anarchist]] kills the [[factol]] of the Mercykillers via a spell, then managed to pin the blame on the [[Fated]]. This time, [[Factol]] [[Mallin]] allows it.{{b|Planescape|The Factol's Manifesto|pdf=17275|page=102}} During the [[Faction War]] of [[130 YFHR]], the extremely charismatic Factol [[Alisohn Nilesia]] had been sold to demonic slavery in the Lower Planes. When the Lady told all factions to abandon the city, the leaderless Mercykillers splintered back into their constituent factions: the [[Sodkillers]] present themselves as the [[Minder's Guild]], a group of bodyguards and mercenaries. The [[Sons of Mercy]], under command of [[Arwyl Swan's Son]], oversee the Prison and attempt to act as a police force, but few recognize their authority. [[File:MimirTheSentinel.jpg|thumb|right|"The Sentinel" by [[Robh Ruppel]]]] A '''mimir''' (mih-MEER), also called a '''Well of Knowledge''' or a '''Speaking Skull''', is a magical item used as a source of information, sort of like a portable [[tout]]. The devices are named after the [[Well of Mimir]] and its proprietor, {{NPC|Mimir|proxy|male|mountain giant|unclassed|0|Fated|n}} the Wise.<ref name="poc-boc115">{{b|Planescape|Planes of Chaos (boxed set)|alt=Planes of Chaos|pdf=17298|nip=1|page=115}}, ''The Book of Chaos''</ref>
Mimirs are repositories of information, either recorded into them by the creator, or recorded by a later user. The most common type of mimir gives a basic overview of the [[Outlands]] and its [[Gate-town]]s. All a user need do is point at it and ask a question: the mimir will click and whirr momentarily while it retrieves the information, and then speak out a relevant recording.
They can also give a rough position in the Outlands, in terms of number of rings out from the [[Spire]], but can't give exact locations.
A mimir follows its user like an ''ioun stone'', but given that it typically marks an [[Outsider (Prime)|Outsider]], it's common to hide it in a satchel or a box unless needed. Mimirs can only be used when freely floating. While a mimir will always float after its user, it otherwise ceases functioning outside of the [[Outer Planes]], only being able to speak gibberish.
A mimir could be in the shape of nearly anything -- a disk, a cube, a star, the head of a sunflower, a leaf -- but the vast majority are in the shape of a skull. Each is about five pounds, and made of a silvery metal with a faint rainbow hue, like the surface of oily water. Looking closely one can see that intricate patterns have been carved all over the surface.
Although mimirs are often available for sale in [[Sigil]] and the gate-towns, they all seem to be second-hand, as no one seems to know where they come from. One mysterious trader in Sigil accepts magical items in trade for a mimir, including cursed items.
Mimir owners are sometimes referred to as "mimir agents," which implies that they're working for the mimir, rather than vice versa.

Factol [[Saladryn]] | sigilhq = | homefield = [[Outlands]] | allies = [[Athar]], [[Fraternity of Order]] | enemies = [[Bleak Cabal]], [[Heralds of Dust]] | predecessor = [[Believers of the Source]], [[Sign of One]] | successor = }} The '''Mind's Eye''' are a [[faction]] formed in the wake of the [[Faction War]], from a merging of the [[Believers of the Source]] (who believed everyone was on a journey toward godhood) and the [[Sign of One]] (who believed that each person was the center of the multiverse), two factions focused on the Self. The Mind's Eye believe they're so connected to the multiverse that they can find themselves only by "finding" the infinite wonder and fulfillment of the planes. Each experience is a stepping stone to personal advancement, even godhood. Or, some whisper, something beyond even that. == History == == Philosophy == The philosophy of finding oneself by traveling the planes is not entirely dissimilar to that of the [[Society of Sensation]], but while the Sensates immerse themselves in the experience, the Seekers -- taking after their Signer predecessors -- tend to view everything at a remove, as though they're the only real people on a stage filled with props and characters there for their benefit. As such they can come across as arrogant and inconsiderate. == Role == == Membership == * ''See also:'' [[List of Mind's Eye members]] ; '''[[Factol]]''' ''Current Factol:'' * Post-Faction War: {{NPC|Ombidias|prime|male|voadkyn|shaman|9|Mind's Eye|ng}}{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=90}} * 5th Edition: {{NPC|Saladryn||female|elf|archmage||Mind's Eye|n}}{{b|Planescape|Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse|page=27}}, ''Sigil and the Outlands''{{b|Planescape|Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse|page=48}}, ''Sigil and the Outlands'' == Background Information == * The Mind's Eye was introduced at the conclusion of ''Faction War'', one of the final products for [[Planescape]] in 2nd Edition. The 2e faction symbol only ever appeared once: on a limited-run TSR Gold promotional sticker sheet sent to some stores alongside Faction War. * [[Ombidias]] is the only relevant factol from 2nd Edition that didn't make the transition to 5th edition, being replaced with [[Saladryn]]. {{former}} [[Dweomerheart]] | language = [[Common]]Although tridrones and higher ranks could speak common in earlier editions, the 5th edition of [[Dungeons & Dragons]] removes the ability of any modron to speak in a tongue other than their native one., [[Modron language|Modron]] | subraces = [[Monodrone]]s, [[duodrone]]s, [[tridrone]]s, [[quadrone]]s, [[pentadrone]]s, [[decaton]]s, [[nonaton]]s, [[octon]]s, [[septon]]s, [[hexton]]s, [[quinton]]s, [[quarton]]s, [[tertian]]s, and [[Secundus|secundi]] | climate = Any | terrain = Any land | height = | length = | wingspan = | weight = | skincolor = | haircolor = | feathers = | eyecolor = | distinctions = | based = | first = }} '''Modrons''' ({{Pronounce|MO|dranz|refs={{Cite dragon/93/Ay pronunseeAYshun gyd|28}}}}) were a race of [[immortal]]s known for their zealous adherence to the principles of law and order above all else. Just as [[fiend]]s were considered the embodiment of evil and [[celestial]]s the embodiment of good, so were modrons the embodiment of the universal principle of order.{{Cite dungeon/186/Creature Incarnations: Modrons}} {{Quote |We are the ultimate law. All other law is tainted when compared to us.
We are order. All other order disappears when held to our light.
We are structure. All other structure crumbles when brought against us.
We are perfect law. |A spokesmodron{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|26}} }} ==Description== A modron's appearance was varied and depended on their position in modron society. The most common appearance of a modron was as a geometric shape, such as a sphere or cube. The amount of sides as well as structure determined a modron's position in their society. The more sides a modron had, or the more complex their structure was, the higher they were ranked. The highest ranked modrons were humanoid in appearance. ==Combat== Modron armies battled the forces of chaos and entropy across the multiverse. They used logic in developing their tactics and followed proven battle strategies. They were relentless in battle, fighting without compassion or remorse, and were willing to sacrifice themselves to achieve their objective.{{Cite dragon/414/Ecology of the Modron|11}} ==Abilities== All modrons were immune to mind-affecting, emotion-affecting, and magic that drew upon the [[Positive Energy plane|Positive Energy]] or the [[Negative Energy plane]]. They were resistant to cold, fire, and acid.{{Cite book/Planescape Campaign Setting/Monstrous Supplement|16-22}} Hierarch modrons had the innate ability to duplicate the effects of ''[[w:c:forgottenrealms:clairaudience|clairaudience]]'', ''[[w:c:forgottenrealms:clairvoyance|clairvoyance]]'', ''[[w:c:forgottenrealms:command|command]]'', ''[[w:c:forgottenrealms:dimension door|dimension door]]'', ''[[w:c:forgottenrealms:teleport without error|teleport without error]]'', and ''[[w:c:forgottenrealms:wall of force|wall of force]]'' spells at will.{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|126}} ==Society== Modron culture was simple. Each modron obeyed all commands given to it by any modron one rank higher. These commands were obeyed without question. Modrons were only aware of modrons one rank higher than they were, for example, a quadrone could issue orders to tridrones, duodrones, and monodrones, but would only obey orders from pentadrones. If a modron higher in rank than a pentadrone issued an order to a quadrone, it would view it as some exceptionally powerful pentadrone. All modrons were aware of the existence of Primus, however. Modrons were unwavering in their devotion to order, departing Mechanus to complete strange tasks in the name of law. The modrons served [[Primus]], godlike ruler of [[Mechanus]]. There were fourteen castes of modrons, divided in two major categories:{{Cite web enhancement/The Modrons|2}} {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center; ! Modron ! Population |- ! style="text-align: center; background:#c5e0b3;" colspan="7" |Base |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Monodrone]] | style="text-align: center;" |300 million+ |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Duodrone]] | style="text-align: center;" |55 million+ |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Tridrone]] | style="text-align: center;" |6 million+ |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Quadrone]] | style="text-align: center;" |1.5 million+ |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Pentadrone]] | style="text-align: center;" |500,000 |- ! style="text-align: center; background:#c5e0b3;" colspan="7" |Hierarch |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Decaton]] | style="text-align: center;" |100 |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Nonaton]] | style="text-align: center;" |81 |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Octon]] | style="text-align: center;" |64 |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Septon]] | style="text-align: center;" |49 |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Hexton]] | style="text-align: center;" |36 |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Quinton]] | style="text-align: center;" |25 |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Quarton]] | style="text-align: center;" |16 |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Tertian]] | style="text-align: center;" |9 |- | style="text-align: center;" |[[Secundus]] | style="text-align: center;" |4 |- |} ===Relationships=== The [[lillend]]i, guardians of the [[Infinite Staircase]], held a grudge against the modrons for reasons unknown.{{Cite book/For Duty & Deity|17}} [[Slaad]]i detested modrons and had waged epic battles against the forces of Mechanus for millennia. ===Religion=== Hierarch modrons were known to occasionally sponsor [[neutral]]-aligned [[witch doctor]]s as [[divine]] patrons.{{Cite dragon/141/Orcs Throw Spells, Too!|33}} ==Physiology== Despite appearing as mechanical constructs, modrons were not entirely mechanical. Every modron had a mix of biological and mechanical parts, the degree of which was determined by their place in modron society. Lower ranked modrons had more mechanical components integrated within them than higher ranking modrons.{{Cite dragon/414/Ecology of the Modron|9-10}} Most modrons had no sense of smell, and no modron had a sense of taste. Modrons used auditory and tactile sensors. Since modrons communicated telepathically while in Mechanus, their sense of hearing was primarily used to detect sounds and to facilitate communication with non-telepathic visitors to Mechanus. Modrons felt pain and physical contact via their tactile sensors and were able to inhibit this as required. All modrons had eyes, with hierarchs having two or more eyes, allowing them to have a full field of vision. Unlike most other creatures, modrons had no need to breathe or consume food and liquid to survive. Modrons required regular intake of a unique form of psychomorphic energy. It had the consistency of thick jelly and emitted a faint inner light. It was harvested by monodrones and stored in a large pool in Regulus. Modrons had to intake this substance every few weeks or else begin to degrade.{{Cite web enhancement/The Modrons|3}} ==History== The [[Giant pantheon|giant deity]] [[Annam All-Father]] acquired the secret of [[rune magic]] for his people from a high-ranking modron by winning a game of lots about a thousand years after the [[giant]]s' [[Thousand Year War]] against the [[dragon]]s.{{Cite book/Giantcraft|58}}
Mechanus and the modrons were discovered by [[Netheril|Netherese]] explorer and [[archmage]] Lady [[Polaris]] around {{Yearlink|-346}}, who also magically bound and employed them as guards.{{Cite book/How the Mighty Are Fallen|3, 31}} Around that same time, a group of properly operating (albeit degraded) modrons had been left stranded in the [[Labyrinth]] in the [[Underdark]] after being separated from the previous [[Great Modron March]].{{Cite book/Out of the Abyss|179-180,183-184}} Modrons were sometimes summoned by [[Calishite]] mages,{{Cite book/Empires of the Sands|50}} and could be encountered in the city of [[Waterdeep]].{{Cite book/City System|25}} ==Appendix== ===See Also=== *[[Great Modron March]] ===Notes=== {{Notes}} ===Further Reading=== * {{Cite dragon/354/Return of the Modrons|35-49}} * {{Cite dungeon/186/Creature Incarnations: Modrons}} * {{Cite dragon/414/Ecology of the Modron|7-15}} ===References=== {{Refs}} ===Connections=== {{Modrons}} [[Category:Animates]] [[Category:Immortals]] [[Category:Modrons]] [[Category:Small creatures]] [[Category:Medium-sized creatures]] [[Category:Large creatures]] [[Category:Creatures of lawful neutral alignment]] [[Category:Creatures found in Mechanus]] [[Category:Creatures]] [[Category:Creatures found in Regulus]] [[Category:Monster]]

==Description== Monodrones were simple spherical constructs with two mechanical arms and two legs. They had a single eye and rudimentary (but functional) wings. They also did not require any food, and drew sustenance from the air around them.<ref name="MM5e-p224" /><ref name="MotPWE3e-p6-7" />
As barely intelligent creatures, they were capable of only one task at a time. They could communicate, but were only capable of delivering a single message consisting of no more than 48 words.<ref name="MM5e-p224" /><ref name="MotPWE3e-p6-7" />
==Personality== Like all modrons, monodrones had an absolute sense of hierarchy and order, and could not be persuaded to disobey their instructions or betray their purpose in any way.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
It was possible, however, for a defective monodrone to go rogue and start acting in its own interests or no longer in accordance with its instructions, sometimes even becoming violent. Such rogues were relentlessly hunted by other modrons, although, unlike their properly operating fellows, they could be reasoned with.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
==Combat== Monodrones were capable of wielding weapons and were competent combatants, although, due to their single-task nature, they were only capable of performing one attack at a time. If destroyed, a monodrone disintegrated completely into dust.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
==Abilities== Like all modrons, monodrones were immune to all effects and spells that influenced the mind, fear and attacks that rely on energy from either the [[Negative Energy plane|Negative]] or [[Positive Energy plane|Positive]] energy planes. They also had a resistance to acid, cold and fire.<ref name="TGMM">{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|126}}</ref>
==Society== Monodrones could only communicate with other monodrones or with [[duodrone]]s. They were incapable of comprehending more advanced modrons.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
As the base of modron hierarchy, monodrones were created directly by [[Primus]] in the [[Great Modron Cathedral]] in the plane of [[Mechanus]]. They were the source for all other modrons, filling the upper ranks by successive promotions when their superiors were destroyed or otherwise promoted.<ref name="MM5e-p224" />
There were approximately three hundred million monodrones in modron society.<ref name="MM21e-p86">{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|86}}</ref>
==History== Sometime in the late 1480s [[DR]], a group of monodrones led by a [[tridrone]] was stranded in the [[Labyrinth]] in the [[Underdark]], separated from the other modrons since the previous [[Great Modron March]], over two centuries earlier. After years of wandering, the monodrones had decayed and lost much of their communication capabilities.<ref name="OotA5e-p179-180,183-184">{{Cite book/Out of the Abyss|179-180,183-184}}</ref>

{{DEFAULTSORT:Cook, Monte}} {{Real-world person | image = File:Monte Cook.jpg | caption = | name = Monte Cook | fullname = | othername = | nickname = | pseudonym = | occupation = Writer, game designer | period = | series = | media = | settings = | works = yes | images = | home = | birthplace = | born = | died = | signature-image = | signature-caption = }} '''Monte Cook''' has been a professional game designer since 1988, working primarily on role-playing games. Much of his early work was for [[Wikipedia:Iron Crown Enterprises|Iron Crown Enterprises]]. During this period, he attracted fan and critical attention with the popular multi-genre setting [[Wikipedia:Dark Space|Dark Space]]. Eventually he took a job at [[TSR, Inc.|TSR Hobbies]], where he was a major contributor to the [[Wikipedia:Planescape|Planescape]] product line. Shortly thereafter, TSR encountered financial difficulties and was purchased by [[Wizards of the Coast]]. Under Wizards of the Coast, Cook was given the project that is now probably his main claim to fame - working as one of the three primary authors, along with [[Skip Williams]] and [[Jonathan Tweet]], of the third edition of ''[[Dungeons & Dragons]]'' (and thus the [[Wikipedia:d20 System|d20 System]] as well). Cook contributed mainly to this edition's ''[[Dungeon Master's Guide 3rd edition|Dungeon Master's Guide]]'', of which he is the credited author.
Cook left [[Wizards of the Coast]] in 2002 and started [[Wikipedia:Malhavoc Press|Malhavoc Press]] to write material for the [[Wikipedia:d20 System|d20 System]] independently. Malhavoc's first product, ''The Book of Eldritch Might'', was an immediate success and is widely credited with demonstrating the viability of PDF publishing within the role-playing industry. This and other early Malhavoc products were initially released only in electronic format, though print versions of most of them have since been released by [[Wikipedia:White Wolf, Inc.|White Wolf, Inc.]]. His most notable work under the Malhavoc banner is probably ''Arcana Unearthed'', a product he describes as a "variant [[Player's Handbook]]".
He caused controversy in mid-2004 by exclusively selling his electronic d20 material with the DriveThruRPG.com store, which then used only the privacy-protected digital rights management PDF system. He eventually succumbed to pressure from his customers to sell his products in standard-PDF form, and DriveThruRPG has more recently done the same.
Malhavoc released [[Wikipedia:Ptolus|Ptolus]], a campaign setting based on his home game which was used as the playtest campaign for the third edition designers, in August of 2006. A huge book (roughly 700 pages, a figure which more than doubles if the accompanying CD-ROM is taken into consideration) featuring some of the highest production values ever seen in the role-playing industry, Ptolus has enjoyed considerable success despite retailing for approximately $120 US, an unheard-of price for a roleplaying product.
Shortly after the release of Ptolus, which Cook has often described as the culmination of his original ambitions for Malhavoc, he announced that he would be focusing on writing fiction and other forms of creative work he has not yet specified, rather than role-playing games, for the foreseeable future.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.montecook.com/cgi-bin/page.cgi?mc_los_157 | title = The Next Chapter | accessdate = 2014-04-07 | author = [[Monte Cook]] | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070501110933/http://www.montecook.com/cgi-bin/page.cgi?mc_los_157 | archivedate = 2007-05-11 }}</ref> White Wolf announced that his final RPG book would be ''Monte Cook's [[Wikipedia:World of Darkness|World of Darkness]]'', his own take on their modern horror setting. It was targeted for a Gen Con 2007 release.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.white-wolf.com/index.php?line=news&articleid=639 | title = White Wolf Announces Monte Cook’s A World of Darkness | accessdate = 2014-04-07 | date = 2006-12-06 | publisher = White Wolf Online | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080419140620/http://www.white-wolf.com/index.php?line=news&articleid=639 | archivedate = 2008-04-19 }}</ref>
